candidate.blueprint_topic: Health Promotion and Maintenance — smoking cessation / disease prevention
candidate.educational_objective: Teach that smoking cessation produces health benefits at any age and that beneficial physiologic changes begin soon after the last cigarette and continue over time.

options.A: Health benefits occur only after at least 10 years of abstinence
options.B: Benefits begin soon after the last cigarette and quitting improves health at any age
options.C: Quitting provides meaningful benefit mainly to younger people with a short smoking history
options.D: Once cardiovascular disease is present, stopping smoking no longer reduces cardiovascular risk

candidate.rationale: CDC states that quitting smoking has health benefits at any age regardless of how long or how much a person has smoked. Positive changes begin after the last cigarette: heart rate drops within minutes, nicotine in the blood reaches zero by 24 hours, and carbon monoxide falls over the next several days, with additional cardiovascular and other benefits accumulating over time. Therefore B is correct. A and C wrongly delay or restrict benefit, and D conflicts with CDC guidance that people with coronary heart disease also benefit from quitting.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Smoking cessation benefits health regardless of age or smoking duration, with physiologic benefits beginning soon after the last cigarette and continuing over time.
candidate.source_locator: Sections 'Health benefits of quitting smoking' and 'Health benefits of quitting smoking over time' — benefits at any age; heart rate drops within minutes; nicotine reaches zero by 24 hours; carbon monoxide falls over several days; cardiovascular risk continues to decline
candidate.source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
candidate.stem: A client who has smoked for many years says, 'At my age, quitting probably would not help much.' Which response by the nurse is accurate?
